newsitem.title: UKRAINE: New Ukraine PM seen as pragmatist, loyal to Kuchma.
newsitem.headline: New Ukraine PM seen as pragmatist, loyal to Kuchma.

text.p: New Ukrainian Prime Minister Valery Pustovoitenko, confirmed in office by parliament on Wednesday, is a close friend of President Leonid Kuchma widely regarded as more of a pragmatist manager-type than an innovator or natural leader.
Pustovoitenko won the support of 226 deputies -- just securing the absolute majority he needed in the 450-seat chamber. Ninety-one deputies voted against him.
Previously a minister without portfolio, the 50-year-old replaces Pavlo Lazarenko, who resigned earlier this month on grounds of ill health.
Pustovoitenko, Ukraine's seventh prime minister in six years of post-Soviet history, is regarded as having good managerial experience and skills but is not seen as a natural ideas man.
Despite being born in the southern Mykolayiv region, Pustovoitenko made his political career in the eastern industrial city of Dnipropetrovsk, also the home city of Kuchma and Lazarenko.
"Pustovoitenko is quite prepared for the job. The only negative factor is that he is also from Dnipropetrovsk," said Volodymyr Pustovoitovsky, deputy head of the parliamentary budget committee.
Kuchma's opponents say Dnipropetrovsk politicians are too dominant.
Pustovoitenko is a personal friend of Kuchma's and headed his electoral staff during 1994 presidential campaign.
Many political analysts say Pustovoitenko is less ambitious than the previous incumbents, Lazarenko and Yevhen Marchuk.
"Leadership is not in his nature," ex-president Leonid Kravchuk said of Pustovoitenko.

But some politicians say his seeming lack of ambition would appear to suit him for the role of carrying out reforms and taking socially unpopular measures, because he may not be overly concerned about his image.
Pustovoitenko is a member of the pro-Kuchma People's Democratic Party, dubbed the "party of power", but he has rarely made any comments on political issues or foreign policy.
The respected Den daily newspaper said on Wednesday he had no clear political position or views.
The newspaper said when Pustovoitenko was mayor of Dnipropetrovsk he ordered a blue-and-yellow Ukrainian national flag to be taken down from the central square where the opposition had hoisted it.
But months later, after Ukraine proclaimed independence as the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Pustovoitenko raised the new Ukrainian flag over his office himself, instead of the red Soviet-era one.

Den said he had given an order to build a monument in Dnipropetrovsk to Ukrainian 19th-century poet and national hero Taras Shevchenko, but at the same time allocated money for flowers to be bought daily for the city's monument to Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin.
"Pustovoitenko never generated any ideas," said Natalya Vitrenko, a leftist deputy. "He is an obedient man."
Pustovoitenko heads Ukraine's Football Federation and tries not to miss any matches involving the national squad or the country's best club, Dynamo Kiev.
Pustovoitenko is married with two children.
